synopsis: Rail and aviation offer precedents from industries that have accepted simulation as evidence longer than road or off-road vehicles, with railway practice providing the booklet’s clearest template for extending validation across heavy off-road machine models and sensor positions [f15358, f15373]. EN 14363:2016+A2:2022 covers railway running-behavior acceptance, including simulated on-track tests and extension to similar vehicles; related validation practice uses at least 24 simulation-versus-measurement comparisons from at least 12 track sections and limits deviations across the whole comparison set [f15362, f15363, f15364]. The proposed transfer is to validate a family model at its envelope corners, document vehicle changes and add targeted bridging tests, consistent with railway guidance on using modified validated models as evidence [f15373, f15365]. EN 50716:2023 is identified as the current railway software standard and successor to EN 50128, but EN 50126, EN 50128, EN 50129 and EN 50716 were not verified in this research [f7717, f7718, f7716]. Aviation contributes tool qualification through DO-330, which does not establish physics-model validity; both DO-178C and DO-330 are listed as not verified [f15367, f15368, f15369, f15374]. ACAS X provides a statistical-simulation precedent involving encounters equivalent to billions of flight hours, with its DO-385 and ED-256 minimum operational performance standards published in October 2018; the booklet emphasizes that aviation acceptance followed years of underlying model development [f15372, f1429, f15374].
